text: In this town, if you say, "I can't wait," you skip right to it. You see, the second you say it, you vanish. You pop back right next to the thing the moment it happens, not a day older. For you, it feels like one second. But if it never happens, you never come back. My twin sister, Tess, has never once said it, until the night she said it to me on purpose. Grandpa said, "I can't wait for the pizza," and popped up on the porch 30 minutes later right next to the delivery guy. Our soccer coach said it about winning a game. That was three years ago. We're still losing. My cousin said it about Christmas in July. His mom put up a tree the next day. Didn't count. It counts what you meant. He popped up under the real tree on Christmas morning. So here we say, "I can hardly wait," even on birthday invitations. Every day after school, Tess and I raced from our gate to the old oak down the street, 100 steps. Right before the end, she'd always grab my hand, so every race was a tie. In March, I climbed the oak for her kite, and the branch snapped. The doctor said I might never walk again. After a month, I quit trying. I shut my curtain so I couldn't see the oak. One night, Tess took my hand, looked right at me, and said slowly, "I can't wait till you walk to the oak tree." Then my hand was empty. Tess never slips. She did it on purpose. If I never walked to that oak, my sister was never coming back. Dad carried me to the oak anyway. Nothing. Mom wheeled me the whole hundred steps. Nothing. It counts what you meant, and Tess meant our race, me on my own legs, gate to oak. So I opened my curtain. Every evening, I held the fence and walked from our gate until I fell, and Mom chalked the step where I landed. The first night she chalked a zero, then three, 12, 40. On our birthday, I blew out the candles alone and froze her half of the cake. By August, I could make it to 80, but the fence stops at 80. After that, there's nothing to hold. In September, I let go. At 90, my knees shook. At 97, I fell. I got up. 98, 99, I touched the oak, and a hand grabbed mine. Tess in her pajamas right next to me at the exact same second. For her, it had been one second. For me, five months. She looked at our hands on the bark and said, "Tie." She's five months younger than me now, so I guess I'm the big brother. That night, we ate her half of the cake, still frozen. Every day after school, we still walk to the oak. Right before the end, she grabs my hand. It's always a tie.
